narrative:
The model estimated a 55.5% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is slightly above the 50% threshold, your application was denied under a process that treats predicted bar failure as an admissions risk. It does not mean failure is certain; it means the decision leaned against admission by a modest margin.

The most influential factor was your law school admission test score. At 34, it is below the accepted-student average of 37.18, but in the context of your full profile its effect actually pushed toward passing. The next strongest factor was your third-year class-rank standing: a decile of 3 versus an accepted average of 5.79, which pushed toward failure. Your first-year class-rank standing, also a decile of 3 versus an average of 6.00, was third in influence and also pushed toward failure. In short, the two academic-rank signals outweighed the favorable test-score signal, producing the slight predicted risk of failing.

Your next step should be to request a review and submit context for the early academic record, evidence of any upward trend or mitigating circumstances, and a plan for bar preparation. Ask whether retaking the admission test would materially help; because the rank signals were decisive, also consider additional coursework or a post-graduate program that demonstrates academic readiness. Reapplying with stronger, updated evidence is reasonable.
